messages.subject: Question about random effects structure
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I was hoping somebody could help me to figure out what the most appropriate random effects structure is for the analysis that I’d like to do. 

I’m using lmer to run a mixed-effects analysis of 7 different experiments. These experiments had originally been run and analyzed individually (using ANOVAs) but we’d like to analyze them together to see if the increased power changes our results.  The experiments are all Picture Word Interference experiments (written word distractor superimposed on a to be named picture target), and we are interested in whether certain properties (FreqA and FreqB) of the distractor influence the reaction times to the naming of the picture (target).

There are 7 experiments and each subject participated in only one experiment.  
Targets vary in how many experiments they appeared in. Some targets appeared in 1 experiment only, others appeared in 5. 
Distractors also vary in how many experiments they appeared in. Some appeared in multiple experiments, others appeared in only 1.
Since FreqA and FreqB are two different (numerical) properties of the distractors, all participants were exposed to multiple “levels” of both variables.

My current thinking is that the model needs random intercepts for subject and experiment.  Subjects are technically nested in experiment but according to Baayen’s textbook and chapter 2 of the lmer book (r-forge.r-project.org/book/Ch2.pdf), lmer automatically detects nesting and deals with it accordingly (I believe the subjects are labeled to allow this to happen).

Typically, we include random intercepts for item, but I’m not clear as to whether item here should be for targets, distractors, or both. Participants made their responses to the targets though the distractors were also present on each of the trials we are analyzing.  FreqA and FreqB, which we care about, are properties of the distractor.  So this is a place that I need clarification about: random intercepts for targets & distractors or both?. Since neither targets nor distractors are fully nested, I assume that lmer would take care of the crossing or targets/distractors with experiment and subject as it always does.

Lastly, I would include random slopes for FreqA and FreqB by subject.

Any thoughts you might have about how to specify the random effects structure would be most appreciated!

Thanks,
Ariel

Hi Ariel,

Based on your description, I would suggest the following guidance: if you want to test whether your FreqA and FreqB effects generalize across targets (respectively distractors), then you should, as you’re thinking, include by-target (respectively by-distractor) random intercepts.  If you don’t include the random intercept, you’re not making that test for generalization.  Whether you have a priori reason to believe that the test for generalization is warranted is, of course, another question, but it sounds like you do have reason to believe that it is warranted.

And yes, including by-subject random slopes for FreqA and FreqB would be appropriate.

Best and I hope this helps!

Roger

messages.body_plain:
To add my two cents:

- Agreed with Roger's suggestion and your interpretation of how to code
that in lmer.
- You might want to play around with nesting Target under Experiment.  This
would basically treat each Target as different for each Experiment.  Same
for Distractors.  In other words, it would model the possibility that the
Targets/Distractors are operating differently in the different experiments.
This may go too far, though, because it would not treat the Targets as
common across Experiments.  Maybe you could even do both, for example,
model both (1|Target:Experiment) + (1|Target), but that might get hairy,
and I haven't ever tried anything like that myself.  It might be
illuminating to try, though.  Either way, this is one of those cases where
I believe that exploring more complex random effects, then using model
comparison to simplify the model if possible can be a good idea.
- You may also want to consider a random slope for FreqA and FreqB by
experiment, e.g. (1 + FreqA | Experiment), to model the possibility that
have different sets of items in a particular experiment (or other
differences between the experiments) could have affected the effects of
frequency.  Again, this might be something worth looking at and then
simplifying out if warranted, but especially if you carefully examine the
random effect estimates and BLUPs, it might tell you something informative
about differences between experiments.

good luck!
-scott

messages.subject: Re: Question about random effects structure
messages.body_plain:
Yeah, and 7 experiments may not be enough for the models to give reasonable
random effect estimates for Experiment anyway.  Maybe, but maybe not.

To me, at least conceptually, Experiment makes sense as a potential source
for random variability, especially if the goal is to aggregate results over
experiments.  Just like there may be random effects by subject, I could
imagine random effects by Experiment (slightly different population,
different times of the year, different lab set up, different experience due
to different collections of items in each experiment, etc. etc.).  One of
the good things about mixed-models is the "partial pooling" of estimates
over different subjects/items, etc., and I think ideally you would want to
benefit from that here, too.  That said, with a relatively low number of
experiments, the model may not fit well enough to be helpful.  I just
thought it would be interesting and worth a try.

I am less sure that Experiment as a fixed effect would be a good thing,
except maybe as a very exploratory kind of analysis (maybe if the random
effect model isn't fitting well).  This is a "no pooling" kind of analysis,
meaning that the estimates for any interactions may be overestimated, or at
least more extreme than we might want to believe.  Unless there is
something clearly different about the Experiments that we are interested in
testing as a predictor, I think using it as a fixed effect may make things
harder to interpret.

So just to be clear, I think the (1+FreqA+FreqB|Subject) + (1|Target) +
(1|Distractor) part of the random effects is the most reasonable "core" to
stick with.  The other stuff (involving Experiment) may help illuminate how
things may be differing across experiments, which seems like a good thing
to examine, since the goal is to try to meaningfully aggregate the data
over the experiments.  But whether it's "necessary" in order to be able to
generalize results to other experiments (which we would normally like to
do!), I'm not suggesting a hard line.

HTH,
-scott

messages.subject: Re: Question about random effects structure
messages.body_plain:
Just a thought regarding this question about whether Experiment should be a random factor: since your manipulations of critical theoretical interest, FreqA and FreqB, vary within Experiment, it is reasonable to ask the question of to what extent the effect size may vary across experiments.  From a hypothesis-testing point of view, including by-experiment random slopes for these factors subjects the fixed effects for these factors to the question of whether the effects of these factors generalize across experiment, under the assumption that the size and direction of the effects may potentially vary idiosyncratically across experiment.  As always, how reasonable that assumption may be is always something that may be open to debate on a case-by-case basis.  This is also a case where it seems to me that a data-driven approach to assessing the presence of a random effect may be appropriate (though keep in mind Doug Bates’s warnings regarding the difficulty of conducting formal significance tests on random-effects parameters).

I agree with Scott about the questionable value of treating Experiment as a fixed effect.  Probably you would not want to include fixed Experiment:FreqA or Experiment:FreqB interactions if your goal is to test the main effects of FreqA and FreqB (and if you did, you would need to make sure to use a true contrast coding, such as sum coding, on Experiment, FreqA, and FreqB, to preserve the “main effect” interpretation of your FreqA and FreqB effects).

Regarding how easy it could be to get evidence for an effect of FreqA or FreqB that generalizes across experiments when you have “only" seven experiments: it may not be difficult at all.  If all experiments have pretty similar effect sizes, you could easily wind up with a highly significant fixed effect even with only seven experiments.

Best

Roger

Yeah, and 7 experiments may not be enough for the models to give reasonable random effect estimates for Experiment anyway.  Maybe, but maybe not.

To me, at least conceptually, Experiment makes sense as a potential source for random variability, especially if the goal is to aggregate results over experiments.  Just like there may be random effects by subject, I could imagine random effects by Experiment (slightly different population, different times of the year, different lab set up, different experience due to different collections of items in each experiment, etc. etc.).  One of the good things about mixed-models is the "partial pooling" of estimates over different subjects/items, etc., and I think ideally you would want to benefit from that here, too.  That said, with a relatively low number of experiments, the model may not fit well enough to be helpful.  I just thought it would be interesting and worth a try.

I am less sure that Experiment as a fixed effect would be a good thing, except maybe as a very exploratory kind of analysis (maybe if the random effect model isn't fitting well).  This is a "no pooling" kind of analysis, meaning that the estimates for any interactions may be overestimated, or at least more extreme than we might want to believe.  Unless there is something clearly different about the Experiments that we are interested in testing as a predictor, I think using it as a fixed effect may make things harder to interpret.

So just to be clear, I think the (1+FreqA+FreqB|Subject) + (1|Target) + (1|Distractor) part of the random effects is the most reasonable "core" to stick with.  The other stuff (involving Experiment) may help illuminate how things may be differing across experiments, which seems like a good thing to examine, since the goal is to try to meaningfully aggregate the data over the experiments.  But whether it's "necessary" in order to be able to generalize results to other experiments (which we would normally like to do!), I'm not suggesting a hard line.

HTH,
-scott

I have a question about the suppressor effect (?) in mixed-effect model. I am using lmer to run mixed-effect model on a sentence comprehension task. I am interested in the interactions between sentence comprehension performance and three independent variables (e.g. variable A, variable B, and variable C).  some previous studies, even if there were a correlation between variable B and the DV, it should be a positive one.

I am confused about how to explain such results. Has anyone met this problem before? 

I would appreciate if anyone could make any suggestion for how to interpret such results.

Many thanks,
Yingying

messages.subject: Re: comparing non-nested mixed models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dan,

Lewis et al (2011) describe a method for non-nested model comparison using a parametric bootstrap Likelihood Ratio Test: 

Lewis, Butler & Gilbert (2011). A unified approach to model selection using the likelihood ratio test. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 2011, 2, 155–162

Basically, if you are comparing Model A and Model B, you conduct two LRT's:
- Estimate the distribution of LR statistics under the hypothesis that Model A is true by generating many simulated data sets using Model A, fitting these data sets using Model A and Model B, and calculating the LR for each pair of models.
- Use the estimated distribution to test how likely the observed LR (or more extreme LR) is under the hypothesis that Model A is true.
- Repeat for the hypothesis that Model B is true.
- If the first test is significant and the second is not, then Model B fits better, the reverse pattern means Model A fits better, and if both tests are significant you're in trouble.
It's computationally intensive, but it's simple to program using 'simulate' from lme4.

best,
Edward

messages.body_plain:
Hmm, I think I may be losing track of the problem.  From your first email,
it sounds like you were finding that A started with a positive effect, but
then when you added B (and C), A stayed positive but B turned negative.

What I'm seeing here is that both A and B create negative effects (and
there's no significant A x B interaction), so I'm no longer sure what
you're asking about.

However, I'm kind of amazed at how small the effects are!  If you
standardized your IVs, then, for example, a change in one standard
deviation of the reading span variable is like a change from a DV value of
2.942 to 2.915, and that's nearly reliable!  Moreover, the fact that the
estimate for the same effect would be a teeny tiny bit smaller on the +B
conditions (e.g., instead of 2.942 vs. 2.915 it would be 2.937 vs. 2.915)
is significant (t = 2.72) is also kind of amazing.  So basically I'm
confused by the scale of the DV, because if your IVs are centered, then
that should mean the intercept is close to the condition mean of the
reference condition (or grand mean, if you centered the A and B variables,
too), but exp(2.9) is only 18, and I doubt the mean RT was 18 ms.  Was it
18 seconds?  Anyway, the point is you may want to look at a histogram of
your RTs and figure out a reasonable transformation.

A few other things to check: do the random effects make sense?  I mean, are
all conditions both within subject and within items?  Assuming digit span
and reading span are properties of the subjects, you could also look at
random slopes of those by item (though not by subject, obviously).

Aside from these things, though, I'm no longer following how these results
fit with your initial description of your problem.

HTH,
-scott
